children: Yes Bank finds itself at a crossroads following the Supreme Court’s recent judgment upholding the January 2023 Bombay High Court decision to reinstate the additional tier-1 (AT-1) bonds aggregating to ₹8,415 crore that were written down in March 2020 by the bank’s administrator.

The SC judgement is a setback for the private bank as the reinstatement of the bonds has adverse implications for its bottomline and core (common equity tier or CET-1) capital. Retail bond holders are reportedly clamouring for the payment of the unpaid coupons on these high-yield bonds.

The bank nearly went belly up in 2020 following a severe deterioration in its financial parameters (in Q3FY20). It had incurred a loss of ₹18,560 crore due to a ramp-up in provisions, including an additional ₹24,766 crore towards bad loans; its gross non-performing assets (NPAs) had shot up to 18.87 per cent; and the CET-1 ratio had plunged to 0.6 per cent as against the minimum requirement of 7.375 per cent. It is now weighing its options to tide over the challenge posed by the SC judgment.

Vinay M Tonse, MD and CEO, Yes Bank, laid all the cards on the table in his recent interaction with analysts. He noted that, based on the bank’s current assessment, which is indicative and as of September 30, the reinstatement of the AT-1 principal amount would have a pro forma impact of about 240 basis points on the CET-1 ratio (which will decline from 13.7 per cent to 11.3 per cent), including profits. Further, the bank’s overall Tier 1 capital ratio is expected to remain around 13.7 per cent on a pro forma basis.

Tonse said: “Capital planning is an ongoing board-level process. Any capital decisions will be based on a careful assessment of regulatory requirements, the cost and availability of capital, shareholder interests, and the bank’s medium-term growth objectives. We will not pre-empt those decisions today.
“For us, the responsibility is to deal with the consequences of the judgment in a disciplined manner while continuing to strengthen the underlying franchise.”

Yes Bank is the first instance of a public-private partnership between major financial entities, led by the State Bank of India, resulting in its revival through a capital infusion of ₹10,000 crore in March 2020.
Tale of missing clause
While the revival has been successful, the write-down of the AT-1 bonds is seeing bond holders kicking up a storm.

The RBI’s March 6, 2020, “draft scheme of reconstruction of the Yes Bank Ltd” contained a specific clause to the effect that instruments qualifying as AT-1 capital, issued by the bank under the Basel III framework, shall stand written down permanently, in full, with effect from the appointed date.

However, the clause was inexplicably missing from the March 13, 2020, “Yes Bank Limited Reconstruction Scheme, 2020” notified by the Finance Ministry. In their judgment, SC judges Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Augustine George Masih said: “We do not, for a moment, think that the central government intended to have the AT-1 bonds written down, having regard to the turn of events right from 3rd March, 2020. Instead, it happened to be the administrator who, in our opinion, acted under an erroneous impression or mistaken belief that reconstruction of Yes Bank by virtue of the reconstruction scheme notwithstanding, he retained the authority to write down the AT-1 bonds.”
The judges opined that the administrator’s action was impermissible and ultra vires the master circular read with the reconstruction scheme.
Procedural lapse

Akshat Khetan, founder of AU Corporate Advisory and Legal Services, said it was hard to fault the judgment on its text: “‘before’ means before (the reconstruction scheme), and the PONV (point of non-viability) power belongs to RBI. Economically, it produces an uncomfortable result.

“AT-1 instruments exist precisely to absorb losses ahead of equity; here, holders of the riskiest paper recover in full while shareholders who were diluted and SBI, which put in capital on the premise the bonds were gone, bear the cost. The bank was rescued and the rescue cost is now shifted not because the write-down was substantively wrong but because it was done a day late by the wrong person. That is an ₹8,415 crore penalty for a procedural lapse.”

He alleged that the deletion of the clause from the final reconstruction scheme did appear as if the government stepped back from the write-down, then allowed the administrator to do quietly what it had declined to do openly.

He described it as an “own goal” for the regulatory machinery, rather than a vindication of AT-1 investors’ risk judgment. “Expect a review petition, tighter RBI templates for sequencing in future reconstruction schemes, repricing of Indian AT-1 paper and, eventually, a negotiated outcome rather than a cheque for the full amount. The auditors’ qualification means the bank cannot sit on ‘evaluating’ for more than a quarter or two,” he said.

Banking expert V Viswanathan observed that if the RBI’s draft scheme of reconstruction of Yes Bank was accepted and notified without the deletion of the write-down clause by the central government, then no court could have interfered as the central bank has the final word on regulatory matters. “A public sector bank infusing capital in a private bank without merging it with itself involves the central government funds and is a good enough condition for invoking the write-down clause. Even after the scheme was notified, had the administrator obtained RBI approval for the write-down, in view of the infusion of equity by SBI and the CET-1 being precarious before the infusion, no court would have entertained any grievance.

“Both options were missed. And the PSB (public sector bank), being an original investor, and now a foreign investor (Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, which took over a part of the SBI stake) suffer,” Viswanathan said.

Venkatakrishnan Srinivasan, founder and managing partner, Rockfort Fincap LLP, observed that Yes Bank’s two AT-1 bond issues, carrying coupons of 9.5 per cent and 9 per cent, have a face value of ₹10 lakh each and are perpetual, unsecured instruments.

“The judgment strengthens investors’ claim to the principal, but does not mean immediate repayment, as the bonds have no fixed maturity. The court has directed that annual coupons be paid in accordance with the respective information memoranda, although the interaction with their coupon cancellation provisions remains an important issue.

“The case also raises serious questions about selling such high-risk instruments to individual investors. In October 2020, SEBI had introduced stricter rules for AT-1 issuance, including a minimum allotment and trading lot of ₹1 crore. These requirements should not be confused with the ₹10 lakh face value of the earlier issues,” he said.

Srinivasan emphasised that the bigger lesson here is that high coupons on subordinated, unsecured AT-1 instruments compensate investors for substantial risks, but do not guarantee income or principal, and the losses can be severe.

Tonse’s observation that the bank is evaluating the implications of the judgment with the same institutional responsibility that guides its other decisions suggests that he will cross the river by feeling the stones when it comes to dealing with the AT-1 bonds challenge.

title: AT-1 bonds: Yes Bank staring at costly ‘procedural lapse’
